“Joseph!! Joseph!!!” He shook his head and tapped it to show what he thought of Joseph’s lack of intelligence.

“But my dear young friend,” said Mr. Pumblechook, “you must be hungry and worn out. Sit down. Here’s a chicken brought from the Boar, and a tongue from the Boar, and one or two other little dishes from the Boar. I hope you won’t think them beneath you. But am I,” he continued, getting up again the instant he had sat down, “really looking at the boy I used to play with in his happy childhood? And may I—may I—?”

He meant, could he shake my hand? I gave permission, and he shook it with great feeling before sitting down again.

“Here’s some wine,” said Mr. Pumblechook. “Let’s drink our thanks to Fortune, and may she always choose her favorites so wisely! Yet I can’t,” he added, getting up once more, “look at such a person—and drink to such a person—without again expressing—May I—may I—?”

I said yes. He shook my hand again, emptied his glass, and held it upside down. I did the same. Even if I had stood on my head before drinking, the wine could not have gone to my head any faster.

Mr. Pumblechook gave me the chicken wing served with the liver, and the best slice of tongue—no awkward dead-end scraps of pork this time—and paid almost no attention to serving himself. “Ah, poultry, poultry!” he said to the bird on the dish. “When you were a little fledgling, you never guessed what lay ahead. You never imagined you’d be a meal under this humble roof for someone who—Call it a weakness if you like,” he said, rising again, “but may I? May I—?”

There no longer seemed much point in repeating my permission, so he went straight ahead. How he kept doing it without cutting himself on my knife, I don’t know.

“And your sister,” he continued after eating steadily for a little while, “who had the honor of raising you by hand! How sad to think she can no longer fully appreciate that honor. May—”

I saw he was about to reach for me again and stopped him.

“Let’s drink to her health,” I said.

“Ah!” cried Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back, almost limp with admiration. “That’s how you recognize them, sir!” I don’t know who this “sir” was; it certainly wasn’t me, and nobody else was there. “That’s how you recognize a noble spirit, sir!”

The first time I got Tom alone, I asked what he’d had in mind during the escape—what he’d planned to do if it all worked and he managed to free a Black man who was already free. He said his plan from the start, if we got Jim out safely, was to take him downriver on the raft and have adventures all the way to the river’s mouth. Then we’d tell him he was free, bring him back home in style on a steamboat, and pay him for his lost time. We’d send word ahead to gather all the Black people around and have them escort him into town with a torchlight procession and a brass band. Then he’d be a hero, and so would we. But I figured things had turned out just about as well as they were.

We got Jim out of his chains in no time. When Aunt Polly, Uncle Silas, and Aunt Sally learned how much he’d helped the doctor care for Tom, they made a great fuss over him, gave him excellent accommodations, and let him have all he wanted to eat, an easy time, and no work. We brought him up to the sickroom and had a grand talk. Tom gave Jim forty dollars for being our prisoner so patiently and doing it so well. Jim was almost beside himself with pleasure and burst out:

“There now, Huck, what did I tell you? What did I tell you back on Jackson’s Island? I told you I had a hairy chest, and what that was a sign of. And I told you I’d been rich once and would be rich again. Now it’s come true, and here it is! There! Don’t you argue with me—signs are signs, remember that. I knew I’d be rich again just as surely as I know I’m standing here this minute!”

Then Tom kept talking and talking. He said the three of us ought to slip away some night, get ourselves an outfit, and go have wild adventures among the Indians out in the Territory for a couple of weeks or so. I said that sounded fine to me, but I had no money to buy the equipment, and I didn’t suppose I could get any from home. Pap had probably returned by now, got it all away from Judge Thatcher, and drunk it away.

“No, he hasn’t,” Tom said. “It’s all still there—six thousand dollars and more. And your pap has never come back since.”

The public always saw these frail, venerable gentlemen in the act of bowing. People generally believed that after bowing one customer out, they continued bowing in the empty office until they bowed the next customer in.

The barrister was sharp enough to recognize that the banker would never have expressed himself so firmly without being morally certain. Unprepared though he was for the large pill he had to swallow, he swallowed it. “And now,” said Mr. Stryver, wagging his courtroom forefinger at the Temple at large once it was down, “my way out is to put you all in the wrong.”

This was a trick from an experienced Old Bailey strategist, and it brought him considerable relief. “You won’t put me in the wrong, young lady,” Mr. Stryver said. “I’ll do that to you.”

Accordingly, when Mr. Lorry called that night as late as ten, Mr. Stryver sat surrounded by books and papers scattered expressly for the occasion, apparently thinking of anything but that morning’s subject. He even looked surprised to see Mr. Lorry and behaved throughout as though distracted and absorbed in other concerns.

“Well!” said the good-natured messenger, after spending a full half hour trying unsuccessfully to bring him to the point. “I’ve been to Soho.”

“To Soho?” Mr. Stryver repeated coldly. “Oh, of course! What am I thinking of?”

“And I have no doubt,” Mr. Lorry said, “that I was right in what I told you. My opinion has been confirmed, and I repeat my advice.”

“I assure you,” replied Mr. Stryver with the utmost friendliness, “I’m sorry for your sake, and for the poor father’s sake. I know this will always be a painful subject for the family. Let’s say no more about it.”

“I don’t understand you,” said Mr. Lorry.

“I imagine you don’t,” Stryver answered, nodding soothingly as if that settled it. “Never mind, never mind.”

“But I do mind,” Mr. Lorry insisted.

“There’s no need; I assure you there’s no need. I assumed there was sense where there is none, and commendable ambition where there is none. I’ve escaped my mistake, and no harm has been done. Young women have made such foolish choices before, often enough, and regretted them afterward in poverty and obscurity. From an unselfish standpoint I’m sorry the matter is over, because it would have disadvantaged me materially. From a selfish standpoint I’m glad it’s over, because it would have disadvantaged me materially. I hardly need to say that I could have gained nothing from it.”
